title: The Diamond Sutra
speaker: Sokaku Kathie Fischer
summary: The main teaching of the dharma talk emphasizes the importance of understanding emptiness and non-attachment, encouraging listeners to cultivate compassion and activism by living in the present moment and letting go of attachments. This approach is rooted in the Prajnaparamita sutras and is illustrated through stories like that of Huineng and Daowu, who demonstrated that true practice involves bringing awareness to life as it is, rather than trying to achieve a specific state. By embracing the present moment and trusting in one's own life, we can find freedom and love, allowing us to engage with others without judgment or expectation.

sentences.text: Now we can hear you.
Well, good morning, Bellingham.
I had so wished to be among you this week, and you are little baseball cards on my computer screen instead.
I've been occupied with a health event that Norman has had this week, and I have not been able to travel.
He was sick, and really unable to care for himself, so I stayed here.
He's getting better, and we expect a full recovery.
He's not all better yet, but I think he's on the mend, feeling much better.
And he made me breakfast.
That's good.
So anyway, I wish I were with you, but it wasn't in the cards for this week.
I would look forward to coming and visiting the Bellingham Zen Center at some point in the future, and practicing with you and spending some time.
So here we have the Diamond Sutra, and I wanted to share some words that I had prepared about it.
For me, some of the cornerstone moments in the Diamond Sutra are in questions like this one that I'm going to read, which is Chapter 11.
*The Buddha said, Subhuti, what do you think?
If there were as many rivers as there are grains of sand in the great river of the Ganges, would the number of grains of sand in all those rivers be great?
Subhuti replied, the number of rivers would be great, Bhagavan, how much more so their grains of sand.*
*The Buddha said, I shall tell you, Subhuti, so you shall know.

If a man or woman filled as many worlds as there are grains of sand in all those rivers with the seven jewels and gave them as a gift to the Tathagatas, the Arhans, the fully enlightened ones, what do you think, Subhuti, would the body of merit produced as a result by that man or woman be great?
Subhuti replied, it would be great, Bhagavan, great indeed, Sugata.
The body of merit produced as a result by that man or woman would be immeasurable and infinite.

The Buddha said, Subhuti, if then a man or woman filled as many worlds as that with the seven jewels and gave them as a gift to the Tathagatas, the Arhans, the fully enlightened ones, and a noble daughter and a noble son or daughter grasped but one four line gata of this Dharma teaching and made it known and explained it to others, the body of merit produced as a result would be immeasurably infinitely greater.*
Or this statement at the end of Chapter 13.
This is the last statement of a similar conversation.

*The Buddha said, furthermore, Subhuti, if a man or woman renounced their self existence every day as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges and renounced their self existence in this manner for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, and someone grasped but one four line gata of this Dharma teaching and made it known and explained it to others, the body of merit produced as a result would be immeasurably infinitely greater.*
In these passages we have a pairing of events.

One is an unfathomable number, almost beyond imagination: the number of rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and of all those grains of sand in all those rivers, the number of worlds filled with the seven jewels, which I looked up.
The list is not always exactly the same, but it's something like this: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, agate or mother of pearl, ruby or red pearl, and carnelian.
Like I said, the list differs a bit.
If all those jewels were given to the Tathagatas, there would be so much merit in that.
Next to this is a son or daughter of good family, which means Buddha family, who learned, understood and shared with others but one four line verse of this sutra.
The merit produced would be so much greater, impossible to fathom.
And why is this?
Because merit is no merit.
That's why we call it merit.
This is the emptiness teaching of the Prajnaparamita.
The words of this sutra, which I've heard and read so many times in my past 50 years of studying, change with each reading.
Now I hear the warmth, the love and a kind of coziness of this emptiness teaching, and how much our lives, just as they are, are expressed here.
We have such busy lives.
Lots of responsibilities.
Lots of work to do, more than we can get to.
Like the grains of sand in the river Ganges.
How are we going to clean up all the sand?
Turn each grain into a river Ganges and gather all those jewels.
How are we going to affect climate change?
What are we going to do about the war in Ukraine, about human trafficking, about all the discrimination, cruelty and violence we witness?
How are we going to get it all done?
Our hearts break every day, thinking of all this suffering and how little we can do to relieve it.
At the same time, we all know that in the midst of that, we can meet a stranger's eyes as we walk down the street, smile and feel the closeness.
Feel how we share everything.
We share the earth's atmosphere, the earth's gravity, the light from the sun.
We are inextricably connected, and when we meet the warm eyes of a stranger in this way, we come home to just this moment of life on earth.
This is the teaching of emptiness.
Our practice is to come home to this moment over and over again, refraining from throwing our attention out to the so-called objects, dharmas, over and over again.
There are no fixed objects, just this moment of human life.

The emptiness teaching, especially through the Diamond Sutra, but also the Lankavatara Sutra, was brought to China in the fourth or fifth century, perhaps earlier, where we find so many wonderful stories that clarify the teaching.
Really, stories of love and coziness and immediacy, unfiltered by our grasping of objects.
But what am I talking about?
Here's the famous conversation between Emperor Wu of Liang and Bodhidharma.
It's in Blue Cliff Record, case one.
It's also in the Shoyu Roku, I think case two.
Emperor Wu of Liang asked the great master Bodhidharma, what is the highest meaning of the holy truths?
Bodhidharma said, empty, without holiness.
The emperor said, who is facing me?
Bodhidharma said, I don't know.
Bodhidharma was a contemporary, more or less, of King Arthur and the Knights of the Round Table, and his life was legendary, just as King Arthur's was.
Bodhidharma left Emperor Wu because his teaching wasn't understood.
So the legend is that he sat facing a wall for nine years.
At one point, he was so angry at himself for being sleepy that he pulled off his eyelids and threw them on the ground, where they sprouted into tea plants.
Camellia chinensis, if I recall.
His disciple Hui Ke cut off his arm and gave it to Bodhidharma to convey his deep sincerity and wish to become Bodhidharma's disciple.
So this is the stuff of legend.
We have no idea what is true, and we have no idea how to find out.
Emperor Wu of Liang was a devout Buddhist.
He had built monasteries, temples, and stupas.
He had ordained many monks and nuns.
So he was asking about the merit of his work.
He had gathered all those jewels, like the number of grains of sand in the River Ganges.

Bodhidharma is suggesting that he not throw himself into objects, not live through so-called objects, not live through past, present, future, not live in a world of projection, expectation, looking for a return on his investment.
Then Bodhidharma's answer to the emperor's next question, who is facing me, is I don't know.
The teaching of not knowing is so dear to us, not knowing.
I believe this not knowing is what Suzuki Roshi referred to with the phrase beginner's mind.
Openness.
Empty of prior judgment or expectation as much as possible.
Here's another emptiness story from China.
A monk asked Zhaozhen, what is Zhaozhen?
Zhaozhen said, non-Zhaozhen.
The monk asked, how can Zhaozhen be non-Zhaozhen?
Zhaozhen said, it is alive.
It is alive.
Last week our grandchildren were here.
We had a wild and crazy fun time.
We watched Jurassic Park together, and we learned that life cannot be contained.
Then we traveled north to walk among the old growth redwoods and the Fern Canyon, the extraordinary place where the Jurassic Park sequels were filmed.
Life cannot be contained.
Total dynamic working, in Katagiri Roshi's words.
Not a thing, not located in a place or a time.
Yet we are alive in a place and a time.
Life is place and time.
This immediacy is the teaching of emptiness.
We also see this in Huay Nang.
Huay Nang is the ancestor who was inspired to go and practice Zen upon hearing of a Gata from the Diamond Sutra.
It's a funny thing.
There's debate about which Gata from the Diamond Sutra he heard.
Most people think it's the one at the end, but some people think, no, no, it's that one in the middle, in chapter I think 14, 13, in chapter 13.
But anyway, there's a debate, and it's so interesting because it's the same matter.
Is the teaching in the Gata?
Is it contained in this Gata and not that Gata?
Are we throwing ourselves into, oh, I better find the right Gata if I want to understand this teaching?
We have this tendency as humans to just throw ourselves: okay, I've got to go find the right Gata.
I don't know if it's this one or that one.
And the teaching itself says no, no.
The teaching incorporates everything we are at this moment, this human life, with whatever we are encountering.
It incorporates.
So whatever the Gata is, the Gata is.
Whatever our moment of life is, our moment of life is.
There's no other.
There's no other opportunity for life.

So with Huay Nang, as we know the story, there's basically a poetry contest, and the favored disciple presents the poem about how we are a mirror on a stand, and our practice is to just continually wipe clean the mirror.
And Huay Nang comes along and says, no mirror, no stand, no dust.
How can we wipe it clean?
And then, of course, we learn that there's the Northern and Southern School, which seem to feature one of those teachings versus the other.
But what has come down to us is that both of those teachings, they're not two teachings, just like the River Ganges.
The work we have to do in our lives feels sometimes like sorting through the sand of the River Ganges.
And our practice is bringing us in contact with our life.
It doesn't make that work go away.
The work is still there.
We still do the work.
The work is going on.
It's always ongoing.
We're always dusting the mirror because we are mirror dusters by nature.
That's our nature.
But with an attitude of being in the present, I'm not blaming the dust.
I'm not thinking I've got to get this job done.
I'm not thinking that if I don't get it done, somebody else is going to see my dirty mirror and I'm going to be so embarrassed.
All those kinds of thoughts are extra.
And we know this.
And sometimes we can smile at ourselves with those thoughts.
So, the Huineng story, and Suzuki Roshi has the beautiful statement, yes, incorporating those two poems: yes, you are perfect just as you are, and you could use a little improvement.
So we know that in human life, we don't have to go this way or that way.
We are complex, always moving, always dynamic creatures, and we can incorporate a lot.
The next story that I wanted to share about the teaching of emptiness is in the Blue Cliff Record in its case 89.
This is a wonderful story for us at this time.
Yunyan asked Daowu, what does the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion use so many hands and eyes for?
Daowu said, "It's like someone reaching back, groping for a pillow in the middle of the night."
Yunyan said, "I understand."
Daowu said, "How do you understand it?"
Yunyan said, "All over the body are hands and eyes."
Daowu said, "You said quite a bit there, but you've only said 80% of it."
And Yunyan says, "What do you say, elder brother?"
And Daowu said, "Throughout the body are hands and eyes."
Sometimes that's translated as "the whole body is nothing but hands and eyes."
So this koan is so beautiful because for me it has the sense of our work in this world.
But it also has the sense that the work is already done.
We do the work, it is already done.
Like the gift of the Tathagata is already given.
We don't have to go shopping for gifts.
The gift is already given.
The work of compassion is already done.
We just show up for it.
We just show up over and over again, no matter what.
Even if it looks hopeless, even if it's difficult, even if it's easy.
Sometimes we don't want to do something unless it's difficult.
But even if it's easy, we should show up for it.
Show up and show up and show up.
Anyway, that's what I have to share with you today.
Studying the Diamond Sutra is like enriching the soil in spring before we plant the seeds and the seedlings.
We are noticing what's already there, has always been there between our feet, beneath our feet rather, under our homes, under our vehicles, supporting and nourishing that which nourishes us.
And these old texts, these original teachings, are so wonderful for us to drop in and visit.
We don't necessarily immediately take to them.
The language is sometimes difficult, but they sink in.

And I think you'll find over time, and I think you have found over time, like I have, that there are these reflections and echoes between these old teachings and the whole history of stories in Zen and in other areas of Buddhism.
And it's so interesting to listen to this 2500-year-old conversation among people in different centuries, commenting on different teachings, commenting back and forth.
And for me, that's the opportunity of the study of the Diamond Sutra, what it brings forth.
And I want to thank Hana for taking it on.
It's a courageous thing to take on something like the Diamond Sutra.

And Hana has done the courageous thing for this practice period and for opening so many doors through which we can take in the teaching, through her beautiful chanting and conversation with others and all the different ways that we can study and all the ways we can touch each other.
And I just want to thank Hana for opening the door and allowing that to happen.
And Hana, your warmth and wisdom and support through this study and through the practice period are dear to us and we are deeply grateful.
And I, too, am deeply grateful for your trust and your understanding, as I have repeatedly intended to be there and then have not been able to be.
So again, thank you.
And I look forward to visiting Bellingham and meeting you all in person at some point, not too far distant future.
Thank you.
Now, I'm finishing early.
Do you take questions on this occasion, or comments?
**Participant:** Sure, we could try that.
Will it take help?
Let's see, can you hear that better now?
Sure, we can try that.
Kathy, can you hear us?
**Sokaku Kathie Fischer:** Yes, I can hear you.
**Participant:** And people on Zoom are welcome, too.
You could unmute and say something.
You could just raise your actual hand since we're all on one page here.
**Participant:** I have a question.
Could you help us, in saying some words, how we can apply the teachings of the Diamond Sutra to the ongoing war in Ukraine, how we can hold it and carry it?
**Sokaku Kathie Fischer:** We don't know.
We can't know.
We can have trust and faith in our practice, our practice which guides us to come back, come back, come back, return to this moment of human life.
Don't turn away into expectation and fantasy and blame.
When we find ourselves in blame, no judgment.
Just come back, come back to this moment.
That's our practice.
It's hard sometimes.
Sometimes it's like an athletic event to come back to this moment.
It's not just like bing, bing, we're back.
No, sometimes we want to remain angry.
We want to engage in hopes and dreams and all the things that we engage.
Come on back.
Take the challenge.
That's our practice.
Come back to this present, to this breath, this body, this moment.
What is here?
What can I do now?
What can I do?
And I think that our activism is, we're in this for the long haul.
The war in Ukraine is not going to be a little blip that gets solved in a month or two or five.
It seems like a long haul.
And to practice in the middle of difficult long haul really takes us to have a lot of faith, a lot of trust in each other, a lot of faith in this practice.
I can come back to this precious life.
I can come back over and over again.
A lot of times when I read these stories about the Zen guys, it's mostly guys, like when Bodhidharma, Emperor Wu did not like Bodhidharma's answer and Bodhidharma left.
He probably had to leave.
He may have escaped out the back with his life.
We don't know.
That's not in the story.
But he left Emperor Wu and he went off for nine years and wouldn't see anybody until [unclear: "Huayca"], according to the legend, chopped off his arm because he wanted to be his student so badly.
So these were really troubled times.
I think it's the third patriarch had to flee and go into hiding.
The third Chinese Zen patriarch had to go into hiding.
And finally, I think it was the fourth, the fourth, I'm getting a little mixed up, the fourth ancestor tracked him down.
The fourth ancestor, I think, was 14 at the time and tracked him down and found him sort of hiding out in the mountains.
I mean, the history of our own lineage is fraught.
And so these events of our time are unspeakably horrible.
And our human history is full of that which is unspeakably horrible.
And so we can look to these, we can look to our own lineage and we can look to other human beings.
Where do we find the energy?
Where do we find the love to give?
Well, it's right here.
It's already given.
We are already alive.
We already have the Earth's atmosphere to breathe, the Earth's gravity to hold us, the sun's light to allow us to be alive.
So that kind of attitude of, I can keep going on forever because I'm surrounded by so many gifts and I have life.
I think that's our kind of practice.
Thank you.
And if anyone else has something to add to that, we would love to hear it.
**Participant:** Kathy, can you hear me?
A little closer.
**Sokaku Kathie Fischer:** Yes.
**Participant:** Thank you.
Hi.
**Sokaku Kathie Fischer:** Hi.
**Participant:** Thank you.
Well, so according to the Diamond Sutra, we wanted you to be here, but you're not here and therefore you're here.
And that's really great.

So I just want to thank you for unpacking a little more, and it gives me hope because there is just this unending gold mine of wisdom that we can tap into and this unending emptiness that we can be a part of bit by bit as we uncover our real nature, our what, original peace, like Robert Aitken said.
And so I don't really have a question.
My question is, will you continue to practice with us, because you have so much to be with us and to share with us.
And thank you.
Thank you for your presence and for your teaching.
I just really love you.
Thank you.
Kathy, can you step back?
Could you step back there?
Now I can see your head.
That's good.
**Participant:** When you talk about life having to live itself, it makes me think of Dogen's and Genjokoan saying life must be the bird and life must be the fish.
But how do we discern the things that life, that we leave to let life be as it is, from the work that we do?
**Sokaku Kathie Fischer:** Could you be more specific?
**Participant:** How do we discern what we try to change and what cannot use a little improvement?
**Sokaku Kathie Fischer:** Well, it's a continual question.
It's not like we find out the answer.
It's like a continual question.
And the attitude Jane shared with me, the teaching of the, Jane, you better help me out.
Anyway, [unclear: "Tessa"] Glassman's work in helping people in the street and elsewhere, he said, you go into the situation not knowing.
You don't go in as the expert.
You don't go in as the authority, as the knowledgeable one, the one with the resources to give resources to the ones without the resources.
You go in with a heart, not just the idea, the heart of not knowing.
And I think with that heart, that's how we learn that this person on the street has the most exquisite wisdom and the most beautiful heart.
And we didn't know that before.

So we go into all of our, as much as we can, we return to going into each moment, especially moment of, that kind of difficult work, within not knowing, not knowing what the outcome should be or certainly will be, not knowing, just being there present, witnessing with open hands.
I think to me that Jane shared that with me, something like that.
I'm rephrasing quite a bit, but that's such a helpful teaching, to bring this not knowing practice into a setting of such challenge and difficulty.
And like I said, I think we all have experienced that moment when you walk down the street and you see a homeless person or a total stranger or whoever, and you connect.
It's like [unclear: "Maureen Stewart"] wrote, she said, when you really see the flower, the flower sees you.
It's an event of seeing.
And I think we know those moments.
And so our practice is to return, to return, to return and not knowing.
**Participant:** That's it, Kathy.
And it's tied in with Glassman Roshi's bearing witness very strongly, that to hold our ground, to feel our feet firmly planted and to just simply bear witness with no judgment.
Someone once asked him, should I give money to a homeless person because they may go buy drugs or alcohol with that money.
And he said,
**Sokaku Kathie Fischer:** and so that's the bearing witness and not knowing.
Yeah.
And we know that's difficult.
That's a difficult practice.
And we are not disengaging our discerning mind.
We're not disengaging our intellect and our discerning mind.
It's just that we're giving that mind its place.
And its place is feet on the ground, held by the earth's gravity, sharing the atmosphere, thriving because of the sun.
Shall we walk?
